title: A Comprehensive Explanation of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life
author: Zhanran
excerpt: True faith and earnest vows are the driving force and the armor of practicing as taught;

inline.s: Unceasingly steeping yourself in the practice, awakening to the meaning of the sutra,
deepening faith and vows, and practicing as taught.
True faith and earnest vows are the driving force and the armor of practicing as taught;
practicing as taught is the fulfillment and the test of true faith and earnest vows.
Reciting often and hearing often, recollecting often and practicing often,
let body and mind gradually enter the Land of Bliss, gradually arrive at the Land of Bliss.
Though for one lifetime you strive diligently and endure hardship, it is but a moment;
afterward you are born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where joy knows no limit.
Remind yourself at all times:
once reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss,
you possess a vajra Narayana body,
forever free of aging, sickness, suffering, and death, receiving only every joy, until you attain Buddhahood.
In study and practice, then, what difficulty could there be that you cannot overcome?

inline.s: [Deepening Faith and Vows, Practicing as Taught]
“Deepening faith and vows, practicing as taught”
is the very core of steeping oneself in the Pure Land teaching. If one truly accomplishes true faith and earnest vows, one will certainly be practicing as taught,
and this is the guarantee that ten thousand practice and ten thousand go
The essential doctrine of this sutra: arousing the bodhi mind and single-minded, exclusive recitation.

The Sutra of Immeasurable Life is the root scripture of the Pure Land school and the ultimate destination of the whole canon of the Tripitaka. Truly is it the Tathagata's teaching of the nature, perfect and complete, the one-vehicle teaching of definitive meaning, the all-embracing gate of every goodness.

[One Vehicle] Also called the one Buddha-vehicle: the only teaching that can bring people to Buddhahood. “Vehicle” means a carriage, a metaphor for the Buddha's teaching, which can carry people across to the further shore of nirvana. [The ultimate destination of the whole canon of the Tripitaka] The ultimate purport (destination) of the teaching of the entire Tripitaka. For the whole Tripitaka simply teaches people to end birth and death, escape the round of rebirth, attain Buddhahood, and deliver sentient beings. And the Sutra of Immeasurable Life is the concrete embodiment of this ultimate purport.

[Perfect and complete teaching] The ultimate and perfectly complete teaching of the Mahayana. [Definitive meaning] The thoroughly ultimate principle. [The all-embracing gate of every goodness] The most all-inclusive gate of entry into every goodness.

Its Dharma-gate of “arousing the bodhi mind and single-minded, exclusive recitation” is perfect and direct, expedient and ultimate, a single leap straight into the goal, the most perfect and sudden of all. It borrows Amitabha's perfect fruit of enlightenment to serve as the causal mind of our own bodhi. Thought after thought we enter the Buddha's fruited enlightenment; mind after mind we dwell in the Buddha's right concentration. Turning from dust to accord with enlightenment, we return from delusion to the real. The mind creates, the mind is: inconceivable.

[Arousing the bodhi mind] Arousing the great mind of “seeking the Buddha Way above (right enlightenment, the attainment of Buddhahood) and transforming sentient beings below.” [Single-minded, exclusive recitation]
always without any other thought
(without any other idea)
reciting the name of the Buddha
(for details, see the article
Single-Minded, Exclusive Recitation
Single-minded, exclusive recitation is also what
Master Shandao taught:
“Thought after thought continuous, to the end of one's life.”
Master Shandao taught:
“Continuity means rebirth
(at the moment of death, one need only keep the thought of reciting the Buddha's name continuous, unbroken by deluded thoughts, and one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss)
. If one can keep thought after thought continuous to the end of one's life
(if one is a person who practices in this way for a lifetime —
that is, a person of single-minded, exclusive recitation
, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.”
(for details, see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching

[Borrowing Amitabha's perfect fruit of enlightenment to serve as the causal mind of our own bodhi] Single-minded, exclusive recitation means borrowing the vast name of Amitabha Buddha's perfect fruited enlightenment to serve as the causal mind of us deluded sentient beings on the bodhi path. — This is the most supremely wondrous point of single-minded, exclusive recitation! [Causal mind] The mind of the causal ground. [Causal ground] From the stage of an ordinary being first arousing the mind to learn the Buddha Way until the perfect attainment of Buddhahood, this whole process is called the “causal ground.”
[Turning from dust to accord with enlightenment] Turning the mind away from the objects of dust and entering the realm of enlightenment.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
When the self-nature is deluded, one is a sentient being; when the self-nature is awakened, one is a Buddha.”
[Returning from delusion to the real] Turning the deluded mind back and returning to the true mind.
(for details, see the article
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha
[The mind creates, the mind is] The Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life says:
“This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.”
[This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha] The Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life says:

“All Buddhas, the Tathagatas, are the Dharmakaya, and enter into the mind and thoughts of every sentient being. Therefore, when you sentient beings think of the Buddha, this mind is itself the thirty-two marks and the eighty secondary characteristics.
This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.
The ocean of the Buddhas' right and universal knowledge is born from mind and thought.”
(for annotation, see
Annotated Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life
[Right and universal knowledge] One of the ten epithets of the Tathagata.
The Sutra of Immeasurable Life has twelve translations in all, of which five survive:
1. The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment, translated in the Later Han by
Lokaksema, abbreviated as the “Han translation”;
2. The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha of Amitabha, the Threefold Enlightenment, the Good and Honorable Buddha, on Crossing Over the Human Realm,
Eastern Wu
translated by Zhi Qian, abbreviated as the “Wu translation”;

[The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha of Amitabha, the Threefold Enlightenment, the Good and Honorable Buddha, on Crossing Over the Human Realm] It means: the sutra in which the Buddha speaks of Amitabha Tathagata delivering the human realm.
[Amitabha]
Amita
, in Chinese translation: immeasurable.

[Threefold Enlightenment, the Good and Honorable Buddha] An honorific title of the Tathagata. [Crossing over] Delivering people, bringing them out of birth and death. The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment (the Han translation) says:
“When I attain Buddhahood, may I be like the Dharma King, crossing over birth and death, with none who is not liberated.”
[Human realm] One of the six realms (devas, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, hells), that is, what is ordinarily called the “human world.”
3. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life, translated in Cao Wei by
Samghavarman, abbreviated as the “Wei translation”;
4. The Assembly of the Tathagata of Immeasurable Life, translated in the Tang by
Bodhiruci, abbreviated as the “Tang translation”;
5. The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha of the Great Vehicle of Immeasurable Life and Adornment, translated in the Song by
Dharmabhadra, abbreviated as the “Song translation.”

The Sutra of Immeasurable Life is also the outline of the whole body of Pure Land scriptures. It sets out in detail the causal process by which Amitabha Buddha attained Buddhahood, the adornments of the Land of Bliss and its inhabitants, the faith, vows, practice, and realization of reborn sentient beings, and the joyful aspiration and renunciation of Pure Land practitioners. This is a scripture that those who recite the Buddha's name must constantly recite and hear, constantly recollect and practice, so that body
(action)
and mind
(thought)
may gradually enter the Land of Bliss and gradually arrive at the Land of Bliss.
Yet
the Sutra of Immeasurable Life has five translations whose contents are not entirely the same. To promote this sutra, then, how should one expound it?

There can be two ways of expounding it: first, to expound the five translations one by one; second, to expound the content of the five translations in a synthesis. The former overlaps in content and consumes time, and the translated names differ from one another, making it hard to know which to follow. So a synthetic exposition is preferable.

A synthetic exposition can also take two forms: first, to unfold it at length; second, to use concise classical phrases, and then to explain them through a modern-language rendering and annotations for each passage.

The advantage of the latter form is this: it is easy to recite and easy to remember, and convenient for steeping oneself in the practice. On a first reading one may read it all in detail; afterward one may read only the classical phrases, consulting the modern rendering and annotations wherever something is unclear. Going a step further, one may leave the modern rendering and annotations entirely behind and simply recite the classical phrases,
unceasingly steeping oneself in the practice, awakening to the meaning of the sutra, deepening faith and vows, and practicing as taught

Reciting the phrases has another supremely wondrous function: recollecting the Buddha and reciting the Buddha's name, perfumed and illumined by the incense and light, causes one's mind and conduct to be right without deviation, pure and undefiled. Thus the karma of defilement decreases day by day, and the karma of purity increases day by day. Once the karma of purity is accomplished, at the end of life one is certain to be born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss.
[Perfumed and illumined by the incense and light] Perfumed and illumined by the incense of virtue and the light of wisdom. Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva says:

“If the minds of sentient beings recollect the Buddha and recite the Buddha's name, then in the present or in the future they will certainly see the Buddha, and will not be far from the Buddha. Without resorting to other means, they will open their minds of themselves. Like one who works with incense, whose body carries its fragrance. This is called the adornment of incense and light.”

(Rendering: if the minds of sentient beings recollect the Buddha and recite the Buddha's name, then in the present or in the future they will certainly see the Buddha and will not be far from Buddhahood. They need not resort to other Dharma-gates; of themselves they will understand the mind and see the nature (open their minds of themselves). It is like one who has been perfumed with incense, whose body carries its fragrance. This is called the adornment of incense and light — adorning oneself with the incense of virtue and the light of wisdom.)
For details, see
Annotated Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva through Buddha-Recitation
Therefore this book adopts the latter form: using concise classical phrases to expound the teaching, and then explaining them through a modern-language rendering and annotations for each passage.

This book aims to spread the Dharma and deliver sentient beings, and so it takes convenience for the many as its rule. It does not strike out on a new path, but rather, on the basis of the five original translations, makes appropriate changes to the already familiar Xia Recension of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, entitling it A Comprehensive Explanation of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, out of respect for the original work.
[Xia Recension of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life] That is
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha of the Great Vehicle of Immeasurable Life, Adornment, Purity, and Equal Enlightenment (the recension),
compiled by Xia Lianju in the Republican period, abbreviated as the “Xia Recension of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life”

For example, in the original book (the Xia Recension), “The Sixth: Arousing the Great Vows” contains twenty-four vows and lists the forty-eight vows. A Comprehensive Explanation of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, drawing on

the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha of Immeasurable Life (the Wei translation), the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha of Amitabha, the Threefold Enlightenment, the Good and Honorable Buddha, on Crossing Over the Human Realm (the Wu translation), and
the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha of the Great Vehicle of Immeasurable Life and Adornment (the Song translation)
, rewrites it as the forty-eight vows (
because
“the forty-eight vows circulate in both ancient and modern times”
—Master Lianchi, Daily Recitations from the Sutras
), and changes the chapter title from
“The Sixth: Arousing the Great Vows” to “The Sixth: The Forty-Eight Vows.”

Again, in the chapter “The Seventeenth: The Merit of Springs and Pools,” A Comprehensive Explanation of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, drawing on the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment (the Han translation), the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha of Amitabha, the Threefold Enlightenment, the Good and Honorable Buddha, on Crossing Over the Human Realm (the Wu translation), the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha of Immeasurable Life (the Wei translation), and the Assembly of the Tathagata of Immeasurable Life (the Tang translation), and
the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha of the Great Vehicle of Immeasurable Life and Adornment (the Song translation)
, makes certain additions and changes to the original book.
Again, certain archaic words (for example, “sou” for “lock” and “hua” for “flower”) have all been replaced with modern words.

Classical phrases have few characters but deep meaning, a single sound but lasting flavor. They must be recited aloud before they are remembered securely, which helps one to understand, to awaken, and to be steeped in them.
The ancients' experience in recitation was this:

“In reading any book, ... one must read so that every character rings out. One may not get a single character wrong, may not miss a single character, may not add a single character, may not reverse a single character, and may not force a memorization in the dark. One need only recite it many times over, and it will naturally come to the mouth and be long remembered. The ancients said: ‘Read a book a thousand times, and its meaning reveals itself.’ This means that when one has read it thoroughly, one understands its meaning without waiting for an explanation. I have often said that reading a book requires three arrivals: the arrival of the mind, the arrival of the eyes, and the arrival of the mouth. If the mind is not here, then the eyes do not look carefully; and if mind and eyes are not single-minded, then one recites at random, and certainly cannot remember, or if one remembers, it cannot last. Of the three arrivals, the arrival of the mind is the most urgent. Once the mind has arrived, how could the eyes and mouth fail to arrive?”
(Zhu Xi, Essentials of Reading)
Zheng Xia of the Song dynasty wrote a poem, Teaching My Descendants to Read:

“Serene and empty, gathered in one, / the will and thought are not scattered. / What the eye sees, the mouth recites; / the ear's awareness secretly hears it. / The spirit silently examines and remembers, / as the mouth tastes what is sweet and rare. / One time through surpasses ten, / and it does not leave one weary.”

The meaning is this: when one is composed and the mind is pure, one's thoughts will not be scattered. What the eye sees is what the mouth recites, and the ear's awareness silently hears the sound. When mind and spirit concentrate in thought and memory, it is like savoring sweet and rare food. Reciting in this way once can surpass the effect of ten ordinary recitations, and one need not be too worn out.

The essentials of reciting the phrases of A Comprehensive Explanation of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life: directly illumine the mind-ground, dissolve everything back into the self-nature, deepen faith and vows, and practice as taught.

[Mind-ground] The mind is the root of all dharmas and can give rise to all dharmas; therefore the mind is called the “mind-ground.” Again, practitioners proceed according to the mind; therefore the mind is called the “mind-ground.” [Directly illumine the mind-ground] Directly remove the deluded thoughts and greed, hatred, and delusion in the mind, so that the mind returns to clarity and purity. [Dissolve everything back into the self-nature] Bring it down to one's own mind and conduct, so that the self-nature turns from delusion to awakening. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
When the self-nature is deluded, one is a sentient being; when the self-nature is awakened, one is a Buddha.”
(for details, see the article
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha
Deepening faith and vows
is extremely important in Pure Land study and practice.
It is the safeguard of practicing as taught
, and
practicing as taught
is in turn the
key

to rebirth in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss. In study and practice, true faith and earnest vows and practicing as taught are like the two wheels of a cart or the paired wings of a bird, complementing each other:
true faith and earnest vows are the driving force and the armor of practicing as taught
(armor for the body)
; and practicing as taught is the fulfillment and the test of true faith and earnest vows.

If one has true faith and earnest vows, one will certainly be practicing as taught; and where there is no practicing as taught, that is precisely the concrete sign that faith is not true and vows are not earnest. Yet true faith and earnest vows are not achieved in a single step (cu, to tread); they must come through long steeping in the practice,
obtained by constantly deepening faith and vows
On
true faith
earnest vows
, and
vigorous practice
, and the relationship among these three, the twelfth Pure Land patriarch, Master Chewu, taught:
“Those without faith, let them be set aside for now
(as for those without faith, let us set them aside and not speak of them)
. Even among those who have faith, to have faith but no vow is still
(is still)
to be without faith. To have a vow but no practice is still
(is still not)
to be without a vow. To practice but not vigorously is still
(is still not)
to be without practice.
The reason practice is not vigorous is that the vow is not earnest. The reason the vow is not earnest is that faith is not true.

In short, true faith is hard to attain. If faith is truly attained, the vow will of itself be earnest. If the vow is truly earnest, practice will of itself be vigorous. With true and earnest faith and vows, together with brave and vigorous practice, one is certain to be reborn in the Pure Land, certain to see Amitabha, certain to realize the three non-retrogressions, and certain to be one lifetime from Buddhahood.”
(for details, see the chapter “26. A Single Thought of True Faith” in
A Discourse on Buddha-Recitation (with Annotations to Master Chewu's Sayings)

[The three non-retrogressions] First, non-retrogression in position, that is, not losing the position one has attained through practice; second, non-retrogression in practice, that is, not losing the practices one cultivates; third, non-retrogression in thought, that is, not turning back from right mindfulness.
Therefore faith, vows, and practice, the three provisions, are the
core
of Pure Land study and practice. The three are an indivisible whole, linked ring within ring, and their relationship is this:
faith awakens vows, vows guide practice; practice fulfills vows, practice proves faith.
These sixteen characters are the
fundamental guideline
of Pure Land study and practice.

That is to say, faith and vows must be carried out in vigorous practice before they are true faith and earnest vows; and vigorous practice is in turn the actual deed that proves faith and fulfills vows, and at the same time the measure by which one checks how true one's faith is and how earnest one's vows are. Those who recite the Buddha's name must:
have true faith and earnest vows, and practice with bravery and vigor.
The Three Character Classic says at its opening:
“In the beginning of man, nature is originally good. Natures are alike; habits draw them far apart.”

The meaning is that at the very beginning, people are all good, and their natures are very much alike. But because each is steeped in the practice under different circumstances, their natures come to differ very widely. Hence the story of Mencius' mother moving house three times: by moving several times in order to choose a good environment for educating her child, she finally brought forth a sage for a generation. From this one can see how great the power of steeping in the practice is:
near cinnabar one turns red, near ink one turns black
What the ear takes in and the eye takes in, what the mind thinks and the body does — this is what steeping in the practice means. Therefore one should
“constantly recite and listen, constantly recollect and practice, so that body
(action)
and mind
(thought)
gradually enter the Land of Bliss, gradually arrive at the Land of Bliss.”
Unceasingly steeping yourself in the practice, awakening to the meaning of the sutra, deepening faith and vows, and practicing as taught.

Please hold this firmly in mind: “Though for one lifetime you strive diligently and endure hardship, it is but a moment; afterward you are born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, where joy knows no limit.”

Every thought we give rise to is a condition for one future rebirth. If we carefully examine the thoughts we give rise to in daily life, and see whether there are more conditions of defilement or more conditions of purity, whether the thoughts of defilement are fiercer or the thoughts of purity are fiercer, then whether we shall be reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss at the end of life will be perfectly clear, with no need to ask anyone else.

Examine carefully whether the thoughts you give rise to in daily life are mostly in accord with the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, and whether those that accord with it are fierce — this is a matter for self-examination! Therefore the work of practicing as taught must be done at the place where the mind arises and the thought stirs.
The Land of Bliss is my home

. When reciting and listening to the phrases, one should add contemplation: the finer the contemplation and the truer the thought, the more one comes to grasp the meaning with the mind. As the patriarchs said: a great tree that leans to the west must fall westward; when the contemplation of one who recites the Buddha's name is accomplished, at the end of life one is certain to be born in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss.
In annotating sutras and treatises, the threefold division into prologue, main body, and transmission is taken as the rule:
1. The prologue section sets out the reasons and conditions that gave rise to this sutra; this is the originating part of the sutra.
2. The main body section sets forth the teaching in response to those originating conditions; this is the principal part of the sutra.
3. The transmission section entrusts the sutra to be transmitted and circulated, and sets out the benefits of transmitting and upholding it; this is the circulation part of the sutra.
This text has forty-eight chapters in all, and is likewise divided into three great parts: the prologue section, the main body section, and the transmission section:
I. Chapters 1 through 3 form the prologue section.
II. Chapters 4 through 42 form the main body section.
III. Chapters 43 through 48 form the transmission section.

To make it convenient to recite in several sittings, this text is divided into two volumes. Volume One begins with “Chapter 1: The Assembly of Sages,” and Volume Two begins with “Chapter 24: Rebirth in the Three Grades.”
Thus have I heard:
This is what I (Ananda) personally saw and heard:

[This is what I (Ananda) personally saw and heard] Because Ananda personally attended this Dharma assembly and was moreover the one who requested it (the person who asked the Buddha to speak the Dharma). [Ananda] In full, Ananda, one of the Buddha's ten great disciples. He was the Buddha's cousin, born on the night of the Buddha's enlightenment, and later left home to follow the Buddha, serving him for twenty-five years as his personal attendant disciple. He was renowned as foremost in much hearing, and many scriptures were recited by him when the Buddha's teachings were compiled. [The ten great disciples] The ten great disciples of Shakyamuni Buddha, namely: Shariputra, foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyayana, foremost in supernatural powers; Subhuti, foremost in understanding emptiness; Ananda, foremost in much hearing; Upali, foremost in upholding the precepts; Aniruddha, foremost in the heavenly eye; Mahakashyapa, foremost in ascetic practices; Purna, foremost in expounding the Dharma; Katyayana, foremost in discussion; and Rahula, foremost in secret practice. [Dhuta] A practitioner who abandons the three kinds of attachment to clothing, food, and dwelling. [Dhuta practices] The practices of a dhuta practitioner. The daily life of a dhuta practitioner must observe twelve rules, called the “twelve dhuta practices.”
At one time the Buddha was in Rajagriha, on Mount Grdhrakuta, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand monks.
At that time Shakyamuni Buddha was on Vulture Peak near Rajagriha, together with twelve thousand great monks.

[At one time] At that time. [Rajagriha] The capital of the kingdom of Magadha in central India. [Mount Grdhrakuta] Also translated as Vulture Peak or Spirit Mountain, situated to the northeast of Rajagriha; it was a famous and auspicious place where the Buddha often taught the Dharma. [Bhiksu] A man who has left home and received the full precepts. [The full precepts] The complete and perfect precepts: two hundred and fifty for monks and three hundred and forty-eight for nuns. [Great monks] A description of these monks as being of very high attainment in practice. [Together] In one place.

All these great sages had already attained the supernatural powers. Their names were the Venerable Liaobenji, the Venerable Zhengyuan, the Venerable Zhengyu, the Venerable Dahao, the Venerable Renxian, the Venerable Ligou, the Venerable Mingwen, the Venerable Shanshi, the Venerable Juzu, the Venerable Niuwang, the Venerable Uruvela-Kashyapa, the Venerable Gaya-Kashyapa, the Venerable Nadi-Kashyapa, the Venerable Mahakashyapa, the Venerable Shariputra, the Venerable Mahamaudgalyayana, the Venerable Kapphina, the Venerable Dazhu, the Venerable Dajingzhi, the Venerable Mahajuna, the Venerable Purnamaitrayaniputra, the Venerable Lizhang, the Venerable Liuguan, the Venerable Jianfu, the Venerable Mianwang, the Venerable Guocheng, the Venerable Renxing, the Venerable Xile, the Venerable Shanlai, the Venerable Rahula, and the Venerable Ananda, who were at their head.

All these great sages had already perfected the six supernatural powers (the heavenly eye, the heavenly ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, the power of unimpeded travel, and the extinction of outflows). They were the Venerable Liaobenji, the Venerable Zhengyuan, the Venerable Zhengyu, the Venerable Dahao, the Venerable Renxian, the Venerable Ligou, the Venerable Mingwen, the Venerable Shanshi, the Venerable Juzu, the Venerable Niuwang, the Venerable Uruvela-Kashyapa, the Venerable Gaya-Kashyapa, the Venerable Nadi-Kashyapa, the Venerable Mahakashyapa, the Venerable Shariputra, the Venerable Mahamaudgalyayana, the Venerable Kapphina, the Venerable Dazhu, the Venerable Dajingzhi, the Venerable Mahajuna, the Venerable Purnamaitrayaniputra, the Venerable Lizhang, the Venerable Liuguan, the Venerable Jianfu, the Venerable Mianwang, the Venerable Guocheng, the Venerable Renxing, the Venerable Xile, the Venerable Shanlai, the Venerable Rahula, and the Venerable Ananda, and they were at their head.

[Supernatural powers] Unfathomable transformation is called the “spiritual”; unobstructed penetration is called the “power.” Here it refers to the six supernatural powers. [The six supernatural powers] The supernatural powers attained by the sages of the three vehicles (sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas), of six kinds: the heavenly eye, the heavenly ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, the power of unimpeded travel, and the extinction of outflows. Specifically: first, the heavenly eye, which can see the sentient beings of the nine realms (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, devas, sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas) dying here and being born there, in their states of suffering and joy, and can see all the various forms and colors of every world without obstruction; second, the heavenly ear, which can hear the speech of suffering, joy, sorrow, and delight of the sentient beings of the nine realms, and all the various sounds of the world; third, the knowledge of others' minds, which can know what the sentient beings of the nine realms are thinking in their minds; fourth, the knowledge of past lives, which can know one's own past lives and deeds in one life, two lives, three lives, and even a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand lives, and can also know the past lives and deeds of every sentient being; fifth, the power of unimpeded travel (the power of bodily ease), by which the body can fly over mountains and seas without obstruction, disappearing from this realm and emerging in that, disappearing from that realm and emerging in this, making the great small and the small great, transforming at will; sixth, the extinction of outflows, the cutting off of all afflictions (the delusions of view and thought), “outflow” meaning affliction. [The delusions of view and thought] The delusion of view and the delusion of thought. The delusion of view is the ordinary being's confusion and error in views, such as the five wrong views of the view of the body, extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of attachment to precepts and observances; the delusion of thought is the ordinary being's confusion and error in thought, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root by which sentient beings drift through the three realms and suffer birth and death to no purpose; cut them off, and one can end birth and death and escape the three realms.

[The three realms] The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world inhabited by sentient beings who have the two desires of lust and food, including the six heavens of desire above, humans and animals in the middle, and hungry ghosts and hells below; the form realm is the world inhabited by sentient beings who are free of the two desires of lust and food but still possess a form body, including the eighteen heavens of the four dhyanas; the formless realm is the world inhabited by sentient beings who no longer have a form body but dwell with their minds and consciousness in profound and subtle meditative concentration, including the four formless heavens (the Heaven of Boundless Space, the Heaven of Boundless Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothing Whatsoever, and the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception). These three realms are all states of birth and death and rebirth for ordinary beings; therefore the Buddhist practitioner first aims to end birth and death by escaping the three realms. [The three vehicles] The sravaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle. The sravaka vehicle is also called the small vehicle: its practitioners, at the quickest in three lives and at the slowest in sixty kalpas, cultivate the Dharma of emptiness and finally, hearing the Tathagata's spoken teaching, awaken to the principle of the Four Noble Truths, cut off the delusions of view and thought, and realize the fruit of arhat; the pratyekabuddha vehicle is also called the middle vehicle: its practitioners, at the quickest in four lives and at the slowest in a hundred kalpas, break through ignorance and finally awaken to the principle of the twelvefold dependent origination, realizing the fruit of pratyekabuddha; the bodhisattva vehicle is also called the great vehicle: its practitioners, through countless kalpas, cultivate the six perfections and further spend a hundred kalpas planting the causes of merit for the thirty-two marks, realizing the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood. [At their head] Those who stand foremost among the assembly.
On

the phrase “all these great sages had already attained the supernatural powers,” Master Huiyuan's Commentary on the Meaning of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life contains the following exchange of question and answer, to resolve the doubts of students:

“Question: ‘Ananda, while the Buddha was in the world, dwelt in the stage of learning and had not attained the extinction of outflows; how can he be named among all these great sages who had already attained the supernatural powers?’ Explanation: ‘Although Ananda dwelt in the stage of learning and could not be called a great sage who had attained the supernatural powers, yet because the great majority were such, the praise is spoken from the majority; therefore it is said that all these great sages had already attained the supernatural powers.’ Question: ‘Ananda's virtue was in truth not yet complete; why must he be listed among this assembly?’ Explanation: ‘Ananda was the one who requested this assembly, and so he must be distinguished and listed. Moreover, Ananda was of sharp and superior faculties; though he dwelt in the stage of learning, he had accomplished immeasurable, supremely wondrous merit, and so he is called a great sage. In the supernatural powers he had definitive understanding to the very end, and so he is also said to have already attained them.’”
Translation:
Question: “While the Buddha was in the world, Ananda dwelt in the stage of learning
(he had not realized the fruit of arhat)

, and had not attained the supernatural power of the extinction of outflows. Why then is the assembly at their head, Ananda included, described as ‘all these great sages who had already attained the supernatural powers’?”

Explanation: “Although Ananda dwelt in the stage of learning and could not be called a great sage, nor said to have attained the supernatural powers, yet all the others were arhats; and so, following the great majority, the praise is given, and therefore it is said that ‘all these great sages had already attained the supernatural powers.’”
Question: “Ananda's cultivated virtue was in fact not yet complete (he had not realized the fruit of arhat); why then must he be listed among these sages?”

Explanation: “Ananda was the one who requested this Dharma assembly, and so he must be listed. Moreover, Ananda was of sharp and superior faculties, understanding a thousand things upon hearing one, never forgetting what passed his ear. Though he dwelt in the stage of learning, he had already accomplished immeasurable, supremely wondrous merit, and so he is called a great sage. As for the supernatural powers, although Ananda had not yet realized the extinction of outflows, he had already understood it thoroughly, and so he too may be said to have attained the supernatural powers.”
Note: In the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha told the bodhisattvas:

“I and Ananda, and the others, before the Buddha King of Space, at the same time aroused the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Ananda always delighted in much hearing, while I always practiced diligently and vigorously. Therefore I have already attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi
(Buddhahood)
, while Ananda protects and upholds my Dharma, and will also protect the Dharma-treasury of the future Buddhas, teaching, transforming, and bringing bodhisattvas to accomplishment.”
From this we may know that Ananda was no ordinary person.

[Dwelling in the stage of learning] Ananda attained arhatship only on the eve of the compilation of the scriptures, and so entered the stage of no further learning. Thus, while the Buddha was in the world, Ananda had not realized arhatship but dwelt in the stage of learning, and therefore had not attained the supernatural power of the extinction of outflows. [The stage of learning] The sravakas have four fruits: stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhat. The first three fruits are “still learning”; the fourth fruit is “no further learning.” The stage of the still-learning is the stage of learning. “Still learning” means one must still advance and cultivate further; “no further learning” means the path of learning is complete and one no longer cultivates.
There were also Bodhisattva Universally Venerable, Bodhisattva Manjushri, and Bodhisattva Maitreya, together with all the bodhisattvas of the Worthy Aeon, and they all came to the assembly.
There were also Bodhisattva Universally Venerable, Bodhisattva Manjushri, and Bodhisattva Maitreya, and all the bodhisattvas of the present Worthy Aeon, who all came to the assembly.
[Manjushri Bodhisattva] A shortened form of Manjushri Bodhisattva, also called
Wondrous Virtue
Bodhisattva and
Wondrous Head

Bodhisattva. [The Worthy Aeon] The past great aeon is called the Adornment Aeon, the future great aeon is called the Star Constellation Aeon, and the Worthy Aeon is the present great aeon; because a thousand Buddhas appear in the world during this great aeon, it is named the “Worthy Aeon.” Our Teacher Shakyamuni Buddha is the fourth Buddha among them. The three Buddhas before him were Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, and Kashyapa Buddha.

blocks.text: Chapter 2: The Virtues of Universally Venerable

inline.s: [Following the Virtues of Universally Venerable] Following and receiving the virtue of Universally Venerable. [The virtue of Universally Venerable] The conduct and vows by which Bodhisattva Universally Venerable, in kindness and compassion, universally aids and delivers all sentient beings.

[Conduct and vows] The conduct of the body and the vows of the mind. Vows are the motive force of conduct, and conduct is the carrying out of vows; the two support each other and thus accomplish great matters.
Conduct and vows must accord; if there is only a vow without conduct, one will never reach the goal or fulfill the vow.
The Treatise on the Bodhi Mind says:
“When people wish to do good or evil, they first set their minds upon it, and afterward accomplish their aim. Therefore one who seeks bodhi arouses the bodhi mind
(vow)
and cultivates the bodhi mind
(conduct)

Among the four great bodhisattvas (Manjushri, Universally Venerable, Guanyin, and Ksitigarbha), Bodhisattva Universally Venerable is renowned for his “great conduct.” The Chapter on the Vows and Conduct of Universally Venerable says:

“At that time Bodhisattva Mahasattva Universally Venerable, having praised the Tathagata's supreme merit, told the bodhisattvas and Sudhana: Good men! Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions, for aeons as numerous as the finest dust-motes of inexpressible, inexpressible Buddha-lands, were to speak in succession of the Tathagata's merit, they could never exhaust it! If you wish to accomplish this gate of merit, you should cultivate the ten kinds of vast conduct and vows.”

[Aeons as numerous as the finest dust-motes of a Buddha-land] Grinding one Buddha-land into extremely fine dust-motes (the finest dust), the number of these finest dust-motes is called “aeons as numerous as the finest dust-motes of a Buddha-land.” [If you wish to accomplish this gate of merit] If you wish to accomplish this gate of merit (the Tathagata's merit), that is: if you wish to accomplish the Tathagata's merit. “Gate” here means a classification of things, as in: to classify by category; this course of study. [The ten kinds of vast conduct and vows] That is, the ten kings of vows of Universally Venerable: first, to reverence all Buddhas; second, to praise the Tathagatas; third, to cultivate offering widely; fourth, to repent of karmic obstacles; fifth, to rejoice in others' merit; sixth, to request the turning of the Dharma-wheel; seventh, to request the Buddhas to remain in the world; eighth, to follow the Buddhas in study always; ninth, to accord with all sentient beings constantly; tenth, to transfer all merit universally.

There were also sixteen true men of virtue: Bodhisattva Virtuous Protection, Bodhisattva Good Reflection, Bodhisattva Wisdom of Eloquence, Bodhisattva Contemplator of Non-Abiding, Bodhisattva Flower of Supernatural Power, Bodhisattva Radiance and Splendor, Bodhisattva Jewel Banner, Bodhisattva Wisdom Supreme, Bodhisattva Root of Stillness, Bodhisattva Faith and Wisdom, Bodhisattva Vow and Wisdom, Bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant, Bodhisattva Jewel Splendor, Bodhisattva Abiding in the Middle, Bodhisattva Restraining Conduct, and Bodhisattva Liberation, who were at their head.

There were also sixteen great bodhisattvas (true men of virtue): Bodhisattva Virtuous Protection, Bodhisattva Good Reflection, Bodhisattva Wisdom of Eloquence, Bodhisattva Contemplator of Non-Abiding, Bodhisattva Flower of Supernatural Power, Bodhisattva Radiance and Splendor, Bodhisattva Jewel Banner, Bodhisattva Wisdom Supreme, Bodhisattva Root of Stillness, Bodhisattva Faith and Wisdom, Bodhisattva Vow and Wisdom, Bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant, Bodhisattva Jewel Splendor, Bodhisattva Abiding in the Middle, Bodhisattva Restraining Conduct, and Bodhisattva Liberation, and they were at their head.

[True men of virtue] Those who cultivate the right Dharma, that is, bodhisattvas. [The sixteen great bodhisattvas] In the pages that follow we shall see that they are all bodhisattvas of the stage of Equal Enlightenment, second only to the Buddhas.

All together they followed and cultivated the virtues of the Great Being Universally Venerable, were fully endowed with immeasurable conduct and vows, and abided in all the dharmas of merit. They roamed through the ten directions, practicing expedient means. They entered the Buddha-Dharma-treasury and reached the ultimate shore.

They all followed and cultivated the virtues of Bodhisattva Universally Venerable (the ten kings of vows), were fully endowed with immeasurable conduct and vows, and abided in the conduct and vows of all merits. Going to the worlds of the ten directions (roaming through the ten directions), they delivered sentient beings according to circumstances by means of provisional and expedient methods (practicing expedient means). They penetrated deeply into the nature (the Buddha-Dharma-treasury) and understood clearly the way to Buddhahood (the ultimate shore).

[Great Being] A general title for bodhisattvas. [The ten directions] East, south, west, north, southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, above, and below. [Practicing expediently] Acting according to circumstances, by provisional means. [Expedient means] The methods, techniques, and language adopted in order to guide and teach sentient beings. The so-called “expedient” is spoken in contrast to the ultimate (the true reality of all dharmas). [The true reality of all dharmas] The actual situation of all dharmas (things and phenomena).
The actual situation of all dharmas is this: ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.
The Sutra of the Buddha-Treasury says:
“What is called the true reality of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever.”
The Mahaparinirvana Sutra says:
“All dharmas are like illusions; the Tathagata, amid them, is undefiled by the power of expedient means.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“The bodhisattva mahasattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, as true reality, neither inverted, nor moved, nor retreating, nor turning.”
(for details, see
The True Reality of All Dharmas
) [The Buddha-Dharma-treasury] That is, the Tathagatagarbha (the intrinsic nature). [The intrinsic nature] The original state of the self-nature, also called the Tathagatagarbha (for details, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha
The following tells of how these sixteen great bodhisattvas will accomplish the Way through the eight marks of Buddhahood in immeasurable worlds of the ten directions (
“aspiring to attain equal and right enlightenment in immeasurable worlds”

[The eight marks of attaining the Way] Manifesting eight marks to attain Buddhahood: descending from Tusita (coming down from the inner court of Tusita), entering the womb, being born, leaving home, subduing demons, attaining Buddhahood, turning the Dharma-wheel, and entering nirvana (entering cessation, passing into extinction). [The Tusita Heaven] The fourth of the six heavens of the desire realm, divided into an inner and an outer court. The outer court is where the devas enjoy pleasures; the inner court is where bodhisattvas of their last life dwell, before descending to the human world to attain Buddhahood.

The following passage tells of the first six marks of the eight: descending from Tusita (coming down from the palace of the Tusita Heaven), entering the womb, being born, leaving home, subduing demons, and attaining Buddhahood.

Aspiring to attain Buddhahood in immeasurable worlds: forsaking Tusita, descending into the royal palace, abandoning the throne and leaving home, practicing austerities and learning the Way. They make these manifestations in order to accord with the world. With the power of concentration and wisdom, they subdue the hosts of demons. They attain the subtle and wondrous Dharma and realize equal and right enlightenment.
They vow to attain Buddhahood in immeasurable worlds:
leaving the inner court of Tusita (
descending from Tusita
), they descend into a royal palace in the human world (
entering the womb
being born
). Then they abandon the throne and leave home (
leaving home

), practicing austerities and learning the Way. They make these manifestations because they accord with worldly conventions (since worldly people have not awakened to the true reality of all dharmas). With the power of concentration and wisdom, they subdue the demon hosts and enemy thieves (
subduing demons
). They attain the profound and subtle Dharma and perfectly realize the Buddha-fruit (
attaining Buddhahood
[Aspiring to attain Buddhahood in immeasurable worlds] A later passage says:
(these sixteen great bodhisattvas)
all obtained the immeasurable merit of all Buddhas, with wisdom and sagely brightness.”

This shows that they, like Guanyin Bodhisattva and Maitreya Bodhisattva, are all bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment, whose next stage of practice is Buddhahood; therefore they vow to go to immeasurable worlds of the ten directions to attain Buddhahood. [Equal and right enlightenment] The Chinese translation of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi: the supreme, true, equal, and universal enlightenment, that is, the ultimate and perfect Buddha-fruit.
The following four passages tell of the seventh mark of the eight: turning the Dharma-wheel.

Devas and humans took refuge and looked up in reverence, and requested the turning of the Dharma-wheel. Always with the sound of Dharma they awakened the worlds, broke through the city of afflictions, destroyed the moats of desire, washed away filth and defilement, and revealed purity and clarity. They tamed sentient beings, proclaimed the wondrous principle, stored up merit, and showed the field of blessing.

After attaining Buddhahood, the sentient beings of heaven and earth all took refuge and relied upon him, requesting the Buddha to turn the great Dharma-wheel. Thereupon the Buddha always used the sound of Dharma to awaken the sentient beings of the world, teaching them to break through the city of afflictions, to destroy the desires that serve as the moat of that city of afflictions, to wash away the defilement of deluded thoughts and attachment, and to reveal their own pure and clear intrinsic nature. He tamed sentient beings, proclaimed the wondrous principle, taught them to accumulate merit, and pointed out to them how to plant the field of blessing.

[The Dharma-wheel] The Buddha's teaching of the Dharma is like a great wheel that can crush all the afflictions of sentient beings. [Destroying the moats of desire] Destroying the desires that serve as the moat of the city of afflictions. Qian (
qiàn
), a moat. [Revealing purity and clarity] Revealing the pure and clear intrinsic nature.

With the medicine of all dharmas, they healed the three sufferings. They ascended the stage of consecration and were granted the prophecy of bodhi. To teach the bodhisattvas, they acted as acharyas, constantly practicing the boundless conducts that accord. They ripened the boundless roots of virtue of the bodhisattvas, and immeasurable Buddhas all together kept them in mind.

With various Dharma-medicines, the Buddha healed the sentient beings amid the three sufferings: those not yet delivered he caused to be delivered, and those already delivered and become bodhisattvas he sprinkled with the sweet-dew Dharma-water of consecration, and granted them the prophecy of when, where, and as what Buddha they would attain Buddhahood. In order to teach these bodhisattvas, he acted as their instructing master (acharya), teaching them constantly to cultivate the corresponding boundless conducts. He ripened the boundless roots of virtue of these bodhisattvas, and immeasurable Buddhas all together kept them in mind.
